Press Release:


SA’s Olympic Stars
All the courage, all the grit, all the glory! Carte Blanche brings you record-breaking action and intimate interviews with 2016 Rio Olympic medal winners. And, intimate insight into the support structures, coaches and family members whose sacrifices have propelled these South African sporting giants into the history books.


Script:


OLYMPIC STARS

V/O: The 2016 Rio Olympics are almost at an end, and South African athletes have bagged 10 medals, making this our most successful Games ever. Silver for swimming star Cameron van den Burgh, a double silver for Chad le Clos, bronze for the Blitzbokke in the Rugby Sevens, silver for Lawrence Brittain and Shawn Keeling in the Rowing; silver for long jumper Luvo Manyango.

Sfx: Eight, thirty-seven.

V/O: Bronze for triathlete Henri Schoeman, silver for javelin thrower Sunette Viljoen, and a sensational gold medal and world record for sprinter Wayde van Niekerk.

Wayde: That last 100m is a miracle, when I look back at my race I’m like “wow, was that me pushing that last 100m the way I did?” even the way I started pulling away the rest of the pack, I mean I still have to pinch myself to think was that me?

V/O: The world was stunned to discover that his coach is a 74 year-old granny from Bloemfontein, but Ans Botha doesn’t know what all the fuss is about.

Ans: I’m a normal South African woman doing what I love and I have a passion for.

V/O: Wayde flew ten members of his family to Rio to watch his event.

Odessa: Once he started running I remember starting screaming. When everything was over I realized I was standing on the woman in front of me’s seat. I was actually holding onto her head or something.

V/O: Wayne’s mother Odessa was also a record setting sprinter in her schooldays, but never competed internationally because of apartheid.

Derek link: Wayde may have broken the 17-year old record of Michael Johnson, but his first challenge started on the day he was born.

V/O: Wayde was born at 29 weeks, weighing just over a kilogram.

Odessa: Then they tell you if he makes it through the next 24 hours he will have one or the other disability.

Wayne: From day one he was a fighter. Me and his mother used to go to the hospital every day, almost for two weeks to see how he lies in the incubator and fight for his life.

Odessa: He was so tiny when we got home for the first time – his grandmother’s sister is a nurse, and she wrapped him in rolls and rolls of cotton wool because he was so, so skinny.

V/O: Wayde donated half a million rand to Groote Schuur Hospital this year and to upgrade the neonatal unit.

The skinny little boy who never gave up on anything became a champ early on, recalls his primary school coach Andre Scheffers.

Anton: In 2003 when he came here he was selected for WP Primary schools team, took part in the South African Primary schools championships up in Polokwane where he became at the tender age of 11, the SA champion under-11 100m sprinter.

V/O: And on the morning of Wayde’s Olympic victory, the whole of Bellville Primary watched the race in the school hall.

Sfx: Screams

V/O: His high school, Grey College, is just as proud of him.

Deon: Although he was also quite a good student academically wise, but he spent most of his extra-mural time training for athletics.

V/O: Wayde is highly competitive but respects his rivals, says step-father Steven Swarts.

Steve: What he always does is he prays for his competitors before the race to keep them whole, so that he can compete fairly. He doesn’t want anybody to get injured while they’re running, because he knows if they can chase him and he can chase them they can push each other to achieve better times.

V/O: Silver medalist Lawrence Brittain also fought against the odds to make it to the Olympics. His mother Danielle is the team doctor, and diagnosed his lymphoma in 2014.

Danielle: We were in shock for a long time, Lawrence don’t forget is an incredibly strong person, so he just said what do I need to do? I said right, you need to stop rowing, you need to put rowing on the back foot and not even think about that. He said right. I said you’re going to commit to the chemo and you’re going to get through this. He said right, I will do everything you tell me. He followed the doctors, he was an exemplary patient.

Lawrence: I think the cancer is a battle. Everyone refers to it as a battle and that’s exactly what it is. It’s not something you can take easily, and it’s seriously tough. I ‘d had six 3-week cycles of chemo and they really knocked me, and I think without the support of the family and friends, the girlfriend and everyone around me, that’s where you get the strength from – you’ve got to have a strong team around you.

V/O: It was 6 months before Lawrence was able to rejoin his team mates and get back in a boat.

Danielle: I remember the cardiologist spending ages with him, looking at his heart and examining it, and then saying “Lawrence your heart’s fine. Go and win medals.”

Shawn: He was back in the boat in March, I mean he was tubby and pale and he had no hair, but he was doing his thing trying to get himself back in the game and get healthy again. He just struggled a bit last year, but this year he’s been a beast, he’s been so strong.

V//O: And together with rowing partner Shawn Keeling, Lawrence managed to hold off every challenger to claim second place in the Olympic final.

Shawn: I’ve known Lawrence for a good time, he’s a good mate and he’s been through a lot. I don’t have words to express just how amazing it is to get it.

Lawrence: It’s definitely worth all the hard work, it’s worth every ounce and every sacrifice we put in.

V/O: And then came Luvo Manyonga, leaping into the limelight with a jump that almost won him the gold medal.

John: He’s a glorious athlete, he is made for the big stage. While other people freeze on the big stage, Luvo loves the big stage. He was born to do this.

V/O: But Luvo almost never made it to Rio. In 2012 he was suspended from competition after testing positive for methamphetamine.

Derek: What are the drugs that really got to you? Was it tik?

Luvo: It was tik yes.

Derek: And what else?

Luvo: There was mandrax and dagga.


V/O; Luvo grew up in Mbekweni, a township outside Paarl. His mother Joyce is a domestic worker, and his father John an unemployed forklift driver.

Joyce: You see this place here is full of tik. The people also use tik, it’s rife in Mbekweni. I said no my child, go to church, don’t use tik. You even said you want to go to the Olympics.

V/O: But in 2014 Luvo’s coach Mario Smith was killed in a car accident.

Luvo: He passed away on his way to come and fetch me and take me out from Mbekweni. He was like my Dad, because when he passed away I lost hope of doing long jump. I went back to drugs, I was like smoking every day.

V/O: While battling his addiction, he worked with strength coach John McGrath.

John: He was battling. Do you know that is one of the great stories to Luvo is that he did battle. Luvo fell more than a hundred times, but he got up that one more time than he fell down.

V/O: Last year Luvo’s father decided to send him to initiation school in the Eastern Cape.

John: I saw my child was drifting. He was born here, and his mates are here. I thought I must take my kid to the bush, there to my father’s house.

Luvo: It changed my life, because they told me that I have to go out there and make my own future and my own family, and I learned a lot. I am now a man, I have to stand for my position and bring something to my family.

V/O: SASCOC President Gideon Sam also intervened.

Gideon: Then I said to him the next thing now is to get out of this township where you are. I spoke to the University of Pretoria, the
High Performance Centre there and they were very keen to assist in having him there.

V/O: It was this leap of faith that carried Luvo all the way to Rio and onto the winner’s podium.

John: The jump, the jump and the medal is like a metaphor, for what he has done is even more significant. Jumping 8.5 metres almost is unbelievable, but what he has done is beyond that again – further.

V/O: Luvo returned triumphantly to Johannesburg to be met by his girlfriend and supporters. He missed the street party in Mbekweni when hundreds of school kids celebrated their hero’s victory. He will avoid the tik-ridden township for now, and focus on his career.

John: If he sticks to his process and where he is, and sticks to his coaches and advice there’s nobody going to touch him. This is going to be the greatest long jumper of all time.

Joyce: I just want to tell the people out there, there is life after anything that happens to you. Just believe in yourself and ask God to help you. God is always there. Today I’m alive and speaking, I have a `silver medal in my name, I put my family name on the map.
